category: theology of God / doctrine of divine attributes
summary: Divine pathos is the theology, central to Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Prophets (1962), that the God of the biblical prophets is not the unmoved absolute of metaphysical theology but a God concerned with, moved by, and emotionally involved in human affairs, so that the prophet is one attuned to and sharing in this divine concern. As Heschel's attributed theology it stands in tension with the classical philosophical doctrine of divine impassibility, and it drew explicit objection from within Jewish philosophy on those grounds.
description:
Divine pathos names the account of God developed by Abraham Joshua Heschel in his study of the Hebrew prophets: the claim that the prophetic literature presents God not as a self-sufficient, unchanging absolute indifferent to the world, but as a God who is concerned, who cares, and who is moved and affected by what human beings do. On this reading, the wrath, the grief, and the compassion the prophets ascribe to God are not mere figures of speech to be explained away, but expressions of a genuine divine involvement with history; and the prophet is understood not primarily as a predictor or an ecstatic but as one who is attuned to the divine pathos and comes to share in it, a stance Heschel calls sympathy. This entry presents divine pathos as Heschel's own attributed theology, in his own vocabulary, and does not assert it as the settled doctrine of the tradition.

Heschel advanced this account in deliberate contrast to a long tradition of philosophical theology, running from the Aristotelian unmoved mover through much of medieval thought, that holds God to be impassible, without change or affection. In the medieval Jewish setting this position is represented by Maimonides, whose doctrine of negative attributes in the Guide of the Perplexed denies that emotions or passions in any literal sense may be predicated of God, and treats the Bible's affective language as accommodation to human understanding. Heschel's theology of pathos consciously departs from this framework, arguing that it imports a Greek philosophical ideal of the divine that is foreign to the prophetic consciousness of Scripture. His position is presented here as his attributed argument, and the Maimonidean and philosophical position it opposes is presented, with equal weight and no ranking, as the attributed classical counter-position.

The theology of divine pathos drew objection from within Jewish philosophy. Eliezer Berkovits, in a chapter devoted to Heschel's theology of pathos, argued that ascribing pathos to God verges on an anthropopathism inconsistent with the philosophical understanding of divine transcendence, and criticized what he regarded as the excess of Heschel's language about God's emotions. Berkovits's critique is recorded here as an attributed counter-position within the internal Jewish discussion, not as a verdict of this entry; the disagreement between Heschel's prophetic theology and the impassibilist philosophical tradition is described, not adjudicated.
editorial_notes:
This entry presents divine pathos as the attributed theology of Abraham Joshua Heschel, in his own terms (neutrality #1, #4, #6): the prophetic God as concerned, moved, and affected by human action, and the prophet as one who shares in that pathos (sympathy). The topic touches the doctrine of God, so the classical counter-position is given equal, unranked weight: (i) the philosophical doctrine of divine impassibility, represented in medieval Jewish thought by Maimonides' negative theology in the Guide of the Perplexed (emotions/passions not literally predicable of God; the Bible's affective language read as accommodation), and (ii) the modern objection of Eliezer Berkovits, who argued Heschel's pathos verges on anthropopathism. Both are recorded as attributed positions; the entry does not rule which is correct (neutrality #2, #7).

relations.note: Heschel developed the theology of divine pathos in The Prophets (1962), an expansion of his Berlin dissertation Die Prophetie (1936): the God of the prophets as concerned and moved by human action, and the prophet as one attuned to and sharing in that pathos. Presented as his attributed theology.

Heschel drew the theology of divine pathos from his reading of the Hebrew Bible, especially the prophetic books, holding that the affective language the prophets use of God expresses genuine divine involvement rather than mere metaphor.

Heschel's theology of pathos consciously departs from the philosophical doctrine of divine impassibility represented by Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed, whose negative theology denies that emotions or passions may be literally predicated of God and reads the Bible's affective language as accommodation. Both are presented as attributed positions; the entry does not rule which is correct.

Both traditions offer an account of prophecy and the prophet's relation to God: Heschel's Jewish theology casts the prophet as one who shares (sympathy) in the divine pathos, the concern of a God moved by human action, while Islamic theology of nubuwwa treats prophethood as the reception and faithful conveyance of divine revelation. Stated as a shared question with differing answers, neither equated nor ranked (neutrality #10-#11).
